claim: Gdf1/3 genes have only been detected in deuterostomes.
source: Gdf1/3 genes have only been detected in deuterostomes (Stenzel et al., 1994; Lapraz et al., 2006; Satou et al., 2008; Simakov et al., 2015; Opazo and Zavala, 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Gdf1/3 is linked to Bmp2/4 in many deuterostome species.
source: The gene is linked to Bmp2/4 in many deuterostome species (Figure 1A; Range et al., 2007; Satou et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1A showing gene arrangements

claim: The linkage between Gdf1/3 and Bmp2/4 is lost in higher vertebrates like mice, chickens, and frogs.
source: though this linkage is lost in higher vertebrates like mice, chickens, and frogs (Opazo and Zavala, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Gdf1/3 originated from Bmp2/4 by a tandem duplication event that occurred in the common ancestor of deuterostomes.
source: Accordingly, sequence similarity and phylogenetic evidence supported the view that Gdf1/3 originated from Bmp2/4 by a tandem duplication event that occurred in the common ancestor of deuterostomes (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Lapraz et al., 2006; Range et al., 2007; Satou et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis, sequence similarity, and citations

claim: Branchiostoma floridae contains two Gdf1/3 genes.
source: However, Floridae amphioxus (Branchiostoma floridae) was reported to contain two Gdf1/3 genes (Satou et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: One of the two Gdf1/3 genes in B. floridae (previously named GDF1/3-like2) is linked to Bmp2/4 and represents the ancestral amphioxus Gdf1/3 gene.
source: one of which (previously named GDF1/3-like2 by Satou et al., 2008) is linked to Bmp2/4 as was found in other deuterostomes, representing the ancestral amphioxus Gdf1/3 gene (hereafter renamed Gdf1/3, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by genomic linkage data and comparison with other deuterostomes

claim: The other Gdf1/3 gene in B. floridae (previously known as GDF1/3-like1 or Vg1) is linked to Lefty.
source: Intriguingly, the other one (previously known as GDF1/3-like1 [Satou et al., 2008] or Vg1 [Onai et al., 2010]), here renamed as Gdf1/3-like (Figure 1A), is also linked to a transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) family gene Lefty (Satou et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by genomic data and citations

claim: The Gdf1/3-like gene and its linkage to Lefty exist only in amphioxus species, but not in any other bilaterians examined.
source: Further survey on recently updated genomes of bilaterians, especially those reported to have Lefty genes, revealed that the Gdf1/3-like gene and its linkage to Lefty exist only in amphioxus species, but not in any other bilaterians examined (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: The Gdf1/3-like gene most likely arose in Cephalochordata through a tandem duplication of Gdf1/3, followed by a translocation to the Lefty locus.
source: These findings suggest that the Gdf1/3-like gene most likely arose in Cephalochordata, or at least in the genus of Brachiostoma, through a tandem duplication of Gdf1/3, followed by a translocation of it to the Lefty locus (Figure 1A).
evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic data and phylogenetic distribution

claim: Lineage-specific duplication of the Gdf1/3 gene and translocation of the duplicate to other genomic regions have been found in at least two lineages of vertebrates.
source: In line with this proposal, lineage-specific duplication of the Gdf1/3 gene and translocation of the duplicate to other genomic regions have also been found in at least two lineages of vertebrates (Opazo and Zavala, 2018; Opazo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: No maternal expression of Gdf1/3-like was detected in amphioxus embryos.
source: Inconsistent with previous study (Onai et al., 2010), no maternal expression of Gdf1/3-like was detected in our analyses (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization, qRT-PCR, and RNA-seq data shown in figures

claim: Zygotic expression of Gdf1/3-like was first detected in the dorsal blastomeres of the vegetal pole at the 32- to 64-cell stage.
source: Zygotic expression of the gene was first detected in the dorsal blastomeres of the vegetal pole at the 32- to 64-cell stage, and then restricted in the dorsal blastopore lip (Spemann organizer) at the gastrula stage and the left side of the embryo from the early neurula stage (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in figures

claim: The expression pattern of Gdf1/3-like is similar to that of Lefty.
source: Notably, the expression pattern of Gdf1/3-like is similar (although not identical) to that of Lefty (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: Supported by comparison of expression patterns shown in figures

claim: No Gdf1/3 transcripts were detected in amphioxus embryos before the neurula stage.
source: Unexpectedly, no Gdf1/3 transcripts were detected in amphioxus embryos before the neurula stage, and very weak expression of the gene was found in few cells of the anterior ventral pharyngeal region during the late neurula and larva stages (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization, qRT-PCR, and RNA-seq data

claim: Homozygous Gdf1/3 mutants displayed normal D–V and L–R axis patterning.
source: Consistent with its restricted and weak expression pattern, the homozygous Gdf1/3 mutants (Gdf1/3−/−) displayed normal D–V and L–R axis patterning as the wild-type (WT) by the 3-gill slit stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis of mutants shown in figure

claim: Gdf1/3 has disassociated from the GRN of body axis formation in living amphioxus.
source: These data suggested that Gdf1/3 has disassociated from the GRN of body axis formation in living amphioxus.
evidence: Inferred from expression pattern and mutant phenotype data

claim: Overexpression of Gdf1/3 results in the expansion of anterior and dorsal identity at the expense of ventral structures.
source: It is, however, notable that overexpression of Gdf1/3 by injecting its mRNA could result in the expansion of anterior and dorsal identity (expressing FoxQ2, Wnt3, Brachyury, and Chordin) at the expense of ventral structures (expressing Evx) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by mRNA injection experiments and marker gene expression analysis

claim: Gdf1/3 still works as a ligand of Nodal signaling.
source: These results demonstrated that the Gdf1/3 still works as a ligand of Nodal signaling, although it is dispensable to the body axis formation of extant amphioxus.
evidence: Inferred from overexpression experiments and inhibitor treatment

claim: Gdf1/3-like−/− embryos showed severe defects in axis formation.
source: Gdf1/3-like−/− embryos showed severe defects in axis formation. At the G5 stage, the Gdf1/3-like−/− embryos failed to flatten dorsally like the WT embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), and at subsequent stages they lacked most of the anterior and dorsal structures (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis of mutants shown in figures

claim: A minority of Gdf1/3-like+/− larvae showed no left but two-right phenotype by the L2 stage.
source: In addition, by the L2 stage, there was a minority of Gdf1/3-like+/− larvae showing no left but two-right phenotype (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis shown in figure

claim: In Gdf1/3-like−/− embryos at G5 stage, the expression of dorsal markers (Gsc, Chordin, Netrin, SoxB1a) disappeared, while ventral markers (Evx, Ap2) expanded dorsally.
source: At the gastrulae (G5) stage of Gdf1/3-like−/−, the expression of Gsc in dorsal mesoderm, Chordin and Netrin in dorsal mesoderm and neural ectoderm and SoxB1a in dorsal pan-neural ectoderm disappeared, while that of Evx in ventral domain and Ap2 in epidermal ectoderm expanded dorsally (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis shown in figure

claim: Gdf1/3-like is indispensable for body axes formation in amphioxus.
source: These data collectively indicated that Gdf1/3-like is indispensable for body axes formation in amphioxus and its loss-of-function leads to loss of dorsal, anterior, and left identities.
evidence: Inferred from mutant phenotype and marker gene expression analysis

claim: In the absence of Gdf1/3-like, Nodal alone could not activate the Nodal signaling in amphioxus.
source: These results suggested that in the absence of Gdf1/3-like, Nodal alone could not activate the Nodal signaling in amphioxus.
evidence: Inferred from Gsc expression analysis in Gdf1/3-like mutants

claim: Nodal is expressed both maternally and zygotically in amphioxus.
source: In amphioxus, Nodal is expressed both maternally and zygotically (Onai et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Nodal−/− embryos exhibited defects of L–R axis.
source: Nodal−/− embryos exhibited defects of L–R axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) as Gdf1/3-like+/− (shown above) and embryos in which late Nodal signaling activity was blocked (Soukup et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis and citations

claim: Zygotic Nodal is necessary for L–R patterning in amphioxus.
source: This result showed that zygotic Nodal is necessary for L–R patterning in amphioxus.
evidence: Inferred from Nodal−/− mutant phenotype

claim: Around 50% and 20% of eggs released by founders 1 and 2, respectively, showed no maternal Nodal mRNA accumulation.
source: In situ hybridization experiment revealed that around 50% and 20% of eggs released by the founders 1 and 2, respectively, showed no maternal Nodal mRNA accumulation (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in figures

claim: Around 50% and 20% of eggs from founders 1 and 2 fertilized with WT sperms (MNodal) showed a mild ventralized phenotype.
source: In line with this, when eggs of the two founders were fertilized with WT sperms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), around 50% and 20% of them (MNodal) showed a mild ventralized phenotype, respectively (Figure 3C, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis shown in figures

claim: MZNodal embryos displayed ventralized phenotypes being more severe than MNodal mutants, but comparable to Gdf1/3-like mutants.
source: MZNodal embryos, as expected, accounting for around 25% and 10% of offspring of the founders 1 and 2, respectively, displayed ventralized phenotypes being more severe than MNodal mutants, but comparable to Gdf1/3 mutants (Figure 3C, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis shown in figures

claim: Maternal Nodal is required for regulating the D–V axis formation in amphioxus.
source: These results collectively indicated that maternal Nodal, probably zygotic Nodal as well, is required for regulating the D–V axis formation in amphioxus.
evidence: Inferred from MNodal and MZNodal mutant phenotypes and marker gene expression

claim: Nodal mRNA injection could rescue Gsc expression in MNodal embryos, while Gdf1/3-like mRNA injection could not.
source: We found that Nodal mRNA injection could rescue Gsc expression in the MNodal embryos, while Gdf1/3-like mRNA injection could not, although it expanded the Gsc expression domain in normal embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by mRNA injection experiments shown in figure

claim: Gdf1/3-like alone (without Nodal) is unable to activate Nodal signaling in amphioxus.
source: This result demonstrated that Gdf1/3-like alone (without Nodal) is unable to activate Nodal signaling in amphioxus.
evidence: Inferred from mRNA injection rescue experiments

claim: The intergenic region between Gdf1/3-like and Lefty could drive reporter gene expression similar to that of the two genes.
source: Further transgenic analyses showed that the intergenic region between Gdf1/3-like and Lefty could drive reporter gene expression as that of the two genes.
evidence: Supported by transgenic reporter assays

claim: The 4 kb intergenic sequence contains sequence elements required for regulating the expression of both Gdf1/3-like and Lefty.
source: These results indicated that the intergenic sequence indeed contains sequence elements required for regulating the expression of the two linked genes.
evidence: Inferred from transgenic reporter assays showing bidirectional activity

claim: Lefty expression depends on Nodal signaling in sea urchin and vertebrates.
source: Moreover, Lefty expression depends on Nodal signaling in these two groups (Saudemont et al., 2010; Bisgrove et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Gdf1/3 expression does not depend on Nodal signaling in sea urchin.
source: while Gdf1/3 expression does not, at least in sea urchin (Range et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Lefty expression in amphioxus embryos depends on Nodal signaling.
source: Additionally, we and others also showed that Lefty expression in amphioxus embryos depends on Nodal signaling (Soukup et al., 2015; Morov et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by current study and citations

claim: The 4 kb region was initially responsible for Lefty expression, and then hijacked by Gdf1/3-like after it was translocated to the current locus in amphioxus ancestor.
source: These results therefore implied that the 4 kb region was initially responsible for Lefty expression, and then hijacked by Gdf1/3-like after it was translocated to the current locus in amphioxus ancestor.
evidence: Inferred from comparative expression patterns and regulatory dependencies

claim: In MNodal embryos, the expression of Gdf1/3-like and Lefty were both significantly reduced or abolished at the early gastrula stages (G1–G3).
source: The result showed that, in MNodal embryos, the expression of Gdf1/3-like and Lefty were both significantly reduced or abolished at the early gastrula stages (G1–G3), although their initial expressions were not affected at the blastula stage (256-cell) and their expressions re-appeared at late gastrula stage (G5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization analysis in MNodal embryos

claim: SB505124-treated embryos exhibited decreased expression for both eGFP and mCherry reporter genes driven by the 4 kb intergenic region.
source: In situ result showed that compared to untreated embryos, SB505124-treated embryos exhibited decreased expression for both eGFP and mCherry genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by inhibitor treatment and reporter gene expression analysis

claim: The 4 kb region includes the sequence elements required for Lefty and Gdf1/3-like expression regulation by Nodal signaling.
source: This indicates that the 4 kb region includes the sequence elements required for Lefty and Gdf1/3-like expression regulation by Nodal signaling.
evidence: Inferred from inhibitor treatment effects on reporter gene expression

claim: The regulatory logic of Lefty expression is conserved in different deuterostomes.
source: Together, these results imply that the regulatory logic of Lefty expression is conserved in different deuterostomes and the regulatory elements used to regulate Lefty expression was hijacked by Gdf1/3-like after its translocation next to Lefty gene in amphioxus ancestor.
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis of expression patterns and regulatory dependencies

claim: Enhancer hijacking events could trigger the evolution of a GRN.
source: The most striking discovery in our study is that enhancer hijacking events could trigger the evolution of a GRN.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings of the study

claim: The GRN of the Nodal signaling pathway in echinoderms and vertebrates represents an ancestral scenario where Gdf1/3 is preloaded in an egg.
source: Thus, the GRN of the Nodal signaling pathway revealed in these species most likely represents an ancestral scenario: Gdf1/3 is preloaded in an egg; by blastula stage, Nodal and Lefty appear zygotically; Nodal functions interdependently with the preexisting Gdf1/3 to activate the signaling pathway, while Lefty restrains the activity of the signaling pathway by inhibiting the signaling (Figure 5; Müller et al., 2012; Montague and Schier, 2017).
evidence: Inferred from comparative data and supported by citations

claim: The conserved GRN of Nodal signaling has been rewired and modified in cephalochordate amphioxus.
source: Our data showed that this highly conserved GRN has been rewired and modified in cephalochordate amphioxus: Nodal is expressed maternally in an egg; ancestral Gdf1/3 lost its expression and function at embryonic stage, while Gdf1/3-like (a duplicate of Gdf1/3) recruited the regulatory elements of Lefty and is expressed in a similar pattern as Lefty from the blastula stage; Gdf1/3-like functions interdependently with the preexisting Nodal to activate the signaling pathway; and Lefty still acts as a feedback inhibitor of the signaling pathway (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by the experimental data from the study

claim: At least three sequential steps are probably required to evolve the GRN as found in extant amphioxus from an ancestral situation: (1) the Gdf1/3-like originated and translocated adjacently to Lefty and hijacked its enhancers; (2) the Gdf1/3 retreated from the Nodal signal; (3) the Nodal became maternally expressed.
source: Our results and those from previous studies in other species enable us to infer that at least three sequential steps are probably required to evolve the GRN as found in extant amphioxus from an ancestral situation as reported in echinoderms and vertebrates (as discussed below): (1) the Gdf1/3-like originated and translocated adjacently to Lefty and hijacked its enhancers; (2) the Gdf1/3 retreated from the Nodal signal; (3) the Nodal became maternally expressed (Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis and evolutionary reasoning

claim: The emergence of Gdf1/3-like would not affect the development and viability of the ancestor of extant amphioxus.
source: Overexpression of Gdf1/3 in zebrafish and Xenopus embryos have no effects on axes development (Dale et al., 1993; Bisgrove et al., 2017). It is therefore expected that the emergence of Gdf1/3-like would not affect the development and viability of the ancestor of extant amphioxus (i.e. step 1, Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from comparative functional data in other species

claim: Disruption of maternal Gdf1/3 function is lethal in sea urchin and zebrafish embryos.
source: In contrast, disruption of maternal Gdf1/3 function is lethal in sea urchin and zebrafish embryos (Range et al., 2007; Bisgrove et al., 2017; Montague and Schier, 2017; Pelliccia et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The retreatment of the Gdf1/3 ortholog from the Nodal signaling could not happen before the emergence of Gdf1/3-like and its recruitment of the Lefty enhancers.
source: This indicates that the retreatment of the Gdf1/3 ortholog from the Nodal signaling (step 2) could not happen before the emergence of Gdf1/3-like and its recruitment of the Lefty enhancers (step 1).
evidence: Inferred from functional requirements and evolutionary logic

claim: Overexpression of Nodal in the presence of maternal Gdf1/3 led to defects in axis formation of zebrafish embryos.
source: Similarly, overexpression of Nodal in the presence of maternal Gdf1/3 led to defects in axis formation of zebrafish embryos (Bisgrove et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Nodal could not become a maternal factor before the retreatment of Gdf1/3.
source: suggesting that Nodal could not become a maternal factor before the retreatment of Gdf1/3 (i.e. step 2 happened before step 3).
evidence: Inferred from functional data in zebrafish

claim: Injection of Gdf1/3 mRNA to the yolk syncytial layer was sufficient to rescue MGdf1/3 defects in zebrafish.
source: Injection of Gdf1/3 mRNA to the yolk syncytial layer, where Nodal is expressed endogenously, was sufficient to rescue MGdf1/3 defects in zebrafish, thus the ubiquitous distribution of maternal Gdf1/3, in the region where Nodal is not expressed, is dispensable (Montague and Schier, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Once the Gdf1/3-like started its current expression pattern by hijacking Lefty enhancers, the function of Gdf1/3-like and Gdf1/3 became redundant, allowing the retreatment of Gdf1/3 from the signaling pathway.
source: Once the Gdf1/3-like started its current expression pattern by hijacking Lefty enhancers, the function of Gdf1/3-like and Gdf1/3 became redundant, allowing the retreatment of Gdf1/3 from the signaling pathway (i.e. step 2, Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from functional redundancy and evolutionary logic

claim: Preloading of a maternal factor (Gdf1/3 in zebrafish or Nodal in amphioxus) could be instrumental for ensuring Nodal signaling initiation in a rapid and temporally reliable manner.
source: As discussed in the study of zebrafish (Montague and Schier, 2017), preloading of a maternal factor (Gdf1/3 in zebrafish or Nodal in amphioxus) could be instrumental for ensuring Nodal signaling initiation in a rapid and temporally reliable manner.
evidence: Supported by citation and comparative reasoning

claim: The establishment of Nodal as a maternal factor may be a compensation mechanism for the retreatment of ubiquitously maternal Gdf1/3.
source: Likewise, the establishment of Nodal as a maternal factor may be a compensation mechanism for the retreatment of ubiquitously maternal Gdf1/3 (i.e. step 3, Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from functional requirements and evolutionary logic

claim: Zygotic Nodal mutants failed to form L–R axis but formed D–V axis normally in amphioxus.
source: Zygotic Nodal mutants failed to form L–R axis but formed D–V axis normally in amphioxus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis of mutants

claim: Maternal Nodal is redundant to compensate the D–V axis formation.
source: suggesting that maternal Nodal is redundant to compensate the D–V axis formation.
evidence: Inferred from zygotic Nodal mutant phenotype

claim: Maternal Nodal mutants formed only partial anterior and dorsal structures.
source: However, maternal Nodal mutants formed only partial anterior and dorsal structures (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3)
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis of MNodal mutants

claim: The expression of zygotic Nodal might be delayed in living amphioxus, compared to that of the amphioxus ancestor before step 3.
source: suggesting that the expression of zygotic Nodal might be delayed in living amphioxus, compared to that of the amphioxus ancestor before step 3.
evidence: Inferred from maternal Nodal mutant phenotype

claim: Enhancer hijacking by Gdf1/3-like was a triggering and probably 'neutral' step for the rewiring of the body axes GRN in amphioxus ancestors.
source: Our proposed scenario highlights that enhancer hijacking by Gdf1/3-like was a triggering and probably 'neutral' step for the rewiring of the body axes GRN in amphioxus ancestors.
evidence: Inferred from the overall evolutionary scenario proposed

claim: Co-expressed gene pairs sharing intergenic enhancers have been reported in various cases.
source: Co-expressed gene pairs sharing intergenic enhancers have been reported in various cases (Ueda et al., 2006; Sumiyama and Tanave, 2020; Zinani et al., 2021; Zinani et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Co-expressed gene pairs often fall into the same functional categories.
source: and often fall into the same functional categories (Zinani et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In zebrafish, the paired her1 and her7 can provide robustness for segmentation patterning.
source: In zebrafish, the paired her1 and her7 can provide robustness for segmentation patterning (Zinani et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The co-expression of Gdf1/3-like and Lefty gene pair achieved by sharing regulatory region likely safeguards a dosage balance between the positive- and negative-feedback loop.
source: The co-expression of Gdf1/3-like and Lefty gene pair (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 2–5) achieved by sharing regulatory region (Figure 4) likely safeguards a dosage balance between the positive- and negative-feedback loop.
evidence: Inferred from the regulatory architecture and functional roles of the genes

claim: The dosage balance between positive- and negative-feedback loops is likely an advantage for robust pattern formation.
source: This is likely an advantage for robust pattern formation as suggested in other gene pairing systems (Zinani et al., 2022).
evidence: Inferred by analogy to other systems and supported by citation

claim: Gdf1/3 is one of the reported examples of small-scale gene duplications in amphioxus.
source: Gdf1/3 is one of the reported examples of small-scale gene duplications in amphioxus (Brasó-Vives et al., 2022), anurans, and mammals (Opazo and Zavala, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: In anurans and mammals both Gdf1/3 paralogs retain the ancestral function in axis formation.
source: However, these genes appear to have evolved differently: in anurans and mammals both Gdf1/3 paralogs retain the ancestral function in axis formation (Birsoy et al., 2006; Andersson et al., 2007; Vonica and Brivanlou, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: In amphioxus only Gdf1/3-like undertakes the axis formation function but Gdf1/3 seems to have lost its original function.
source: while in amphioxus only Gdf1/3-like undertakes this function but Gdf1/3 seems to have lost its original function.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data from the study

claim: Hijacking of Lefty enhancers by Gdf1/3-like had enabled Gdf1/3-like to be functionally redundant to Gdf1/3, allowing Gdf1/3 to retrieve from its ancestral function in regulating body axis formation through changing its expression pattern.
source: As discussed above, hijacking of Lefty enhancers by Gdf1/3-like had enabled Gdf1/3-like to be functionally redundant to Gdf1/3, allowing Gdf1/3 to retrieve from its ancestral function in regulating body axis formation through changing its expression pattern.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings and evolutionary scenario

claim: The redundancy of Gdf1/3-like appears to have also relaxed the selection pressure on Gdf1/3-coding region.
source: In addition, the redundancy of Gdf1/3-like appears to have also relaxed the selection pressure on Gdf1/3-coding region, since Gdf1/3-like mRNA is more efficient in inducing anterior and dorsal expansion than that of Gdf1/3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from functional comparison of Gdf1/3 and Gdf1/3-like

claim: Nodal signaling plays a conserved role in patterning the dorsal–ventral (D–V) and left–right (L–R) axes in deuterostomes.
source: Nodal signaling plays a conserved role in patterning the dorsal–ventral (D–V) and left–right (L–R) axes in deuterostomes, exhibiting a conserved GRN orchestrated principally by Nodal, Gdf1/3, and Lefty (Jia and Meng, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Mammals and frogs have two Gdf1/3 genes (namely Gdf1 and Gdf3), derived from lineage-specific duplications.
source: Different from most deuterostomes which has one Gdf1/3 gene, mammals and frogs have two such genes (namely Gdf1 and Gdf3), derived from lineage-specific duplications (Opazo and Zavala, 2018; Opazo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Nodal is expressed zygotically (unilaterally at neurula or larva stage) in echinoderms and vertebrates.
source: The expression patterns of genes coding Nodal and Gdf1/3 are highly conserved in echinoderms and vertebrates, with Nodal being expressed zygotically (unilaterally at neurula or larva stage) (Supplementary file 1a)
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary data

claim: Gdf1/3 is expressed both maternally and zygotically (but bilaterally at neurula stage) in echinoderms and vertebrates.
source: and Gdf1/3 both maternally and zygotically (but bilaterally at neurula stage) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary data

claim: Zygotic Nodal functions synergistically with preexisting maternal Gdf1/3 by forming heterodimers to activate the signaling pathway.
source: Zygotic Nodal functions synergistically with preexisting maternal Gdf1/3 by forming heterodimers to activate the signaling pathway (Montague and Schier, 2017; Opazo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Robust Nodal signaling is safeguarded by a positive-feedback loop from further activation of Nodal itself and a negative feedback loop through inducing the expression of Lefty.
source: Robust Nodal signaling is safeguarded by a positive-feedback loop from further activation of Nodal itself and a negative feedback loop through inducing the expression of Lefty encoding an inhibitor of the signaling (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Lefty gene in amphioxus is expressed zygotically and unilaterally.
source: Like the orthologs in echinoderms (Duboc et al., 2008) and vertebrates (Meno et al., 1997; Bisgrove et al., 1999; Ishimaru et al., 2000; Tanegashima et al., 2000), Lefty gene in amphioxus is expressed zygotically and unilaterally (Onai et al., 2010; Soukup et al., 2015; Morov et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Nodal and GDF1/3-like1/Vg1 are both maternally supplied and zygotically expressed unilaterally at the neurula stage in amphioxus.
source: Unusually, it was found that Nodal and GDF1/3-like1/Vg1 are both maternally supplied and zygotically expressed unilaterally at the neurula stage (Supplementary file 1a and b).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary data and previous studies

claim: The regulatory network governing the Nodal signaling pathway has undergone alterations within the amphioxus clade, while its function in D–V and L–R axes patterning has been preserved.
source: This implies that the regulatory network governing the Nodal signaling pathway has undergone alterations within this particular clade, while its function in D–V and L–R axes patterning has been preserved (Onai et al., 2010; Soukup et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from expression pattern differences and supported by citations
